axes.brief:
Competitive elected institutions, legislative recall and constitutional judicial review coexist with electoral irregularities and weak accountability.
Focused six-question reassessment: Elected presidential government and technical administration coexist with weak accountability. Petitions and recall do not create a general binding national-law initiative, and the public presidential mandate is not a freely transferable party office.
axes.counterEvidence:
Formal checks are real but not uniformly independent in practice; future2027election arrangements and proposed constitutional changes are not completed events.
The owner-defined broader axis includes lawful delegation and direct public control; a lower numerical placement is not a regime classification. Six exact responses and response strengths remain inferred. Retained source access dates are not refreshed unless a source was actually revisited. Unchanged answers and other axes were not re-audited. Elected presidential government and technical administration coexist with weak accountability. Petitions and recall do not create a general binding national-law initiative, and the public presidential mandate is not a freely transferable party office.

answers.rationale: Competitive elections and fixed elected terms operate, qualified by irregularities and unequal electoral practice. Current2026off-cycle votes and2027general timetable corroborate continued elections.

Educated assumption: Agree is the most likely response to the revised claim “Important national policy decisions should be delegated to independent experts who do not need approval from elected representatives for each decision.” in the specified scope (Contemporary institutions and implemented policy; intended cut-off 2026-10-04). The retained sourced research records: Competitive elected institutions, legislative recall and constitutional judicial review coexist with electoral irregularities and weak accountability. Focused interpretation: Elected presidential government and technical administration coexist with weak accountability. Petitions and recall do not create a general binding national-law initiative, and the public presidential mandate is not a freely transferable party office. This is delegation of policy decisions to independent specialists, not replacement of the electorate or a claim that all expertise is political sovereignty. A legislative mandate, appointment process and later review can coexist with not voting on every operational decision.  The described institutional delegation or bounded permission makes agreement more likely than disagreement. Legal safeguards, narrower implementation or an inferred historical application make ordinary agreement more appropriate than an unconditional strong response. The citations supply contextual evidence, not a documented exact response to this new wording. The original source dossier is used as retained research; this pass does not claim a fresh retrieval or complete verification of every historical citation. Precise policy scope, hypothetical institutional translations and response intensity remain uncertain.
